calibration.reference_10: Seeing Theory (Brown University), 'Frequentist Inference' and 'Regression Analysis' chapters — every concept is a live model the learner drives, the sampling distribution builds up in front of you, and there is no sentence a statistician would strike.

caps_triggered.evidence: app.js:245 keyed feedback says late-library students are 'around two-thirds of everyone leaving the library at 21:00'; the convenience pool in data.js:65-72 is 302 late-library of 531 (56.9%), and the learner's own table shows 55–58% at n≥200 (drawSample convenience 500 → 56.4%). index.html:81 lets the axis minimum reach 72 while the data minimum is 71.0; app.js:126 clamps off-scale values to the axis floor, so at min=72 the whole Group B line and two Group A points are drawn at 72 while the end label prints '71.8' — a chart whose picture disagrees with its own numbers. Also index.html:276 example limitation 'temperature was inferred, not measured directly' is false: weeks[].tempC is a measured field and the data table shows a Temp (°C) column. EDUCATOR_GUIDE.md:20 claims r 'is introduced as how tightly two things move together, from −1 to 1'; no such sentence exists in index.html or app.js.

verdict: Statistically literate and honest in its nuance — non-zero axes, bias versus size, common cause, and free text handled without fake grading — but the numbers in the copy do not all survive checking: the sampling feedback says 'around two-thirds' where the data give 57%, the framing slider can push Group B off-scale so the chart draws 71.8 on the 72 floor, and the guide claims r is defined when the lesson never defines it. All three experiments are optional and the keyed option is always the longest, so a test-wise learner finishes without moving a slider, drawing a sample or splitting by season. Fix the numbers, gate each check on its experiment, label the lines and define r, and this is a 7.

gap_to_10: Seeing Theory (Brown). Its sampling chapter makes the learner predict, then watches a distribution of sample means accumulate live so bias (a shifted pile) and variance (a wide pile) become two visibly different things; here the learner gets discrete dots on a fixed 6–8 axis and a paragraph. Its explainers never show a coefficient before defining it, never let a control drive a point off the drawable range, and never state a number the underlying data contradict. And its questions cannot be answered by picking the longest option — the model must be run to know.
